title: Writing as an Iterative Process: From First Draft to Final Version
brief: Explain the core idea that writing is a process involving multiple drafts rather than a single finished product. Draw on the source's statement that providing students with written feedback on their papers and allowing them to revise their work shows students that writing is a process and may involve writing multiple drafts. Describe how formative feedback shapes changes in subsequent drafts, while summative feedback is applied to final versions, using the source's distinction between these two types of teacher response. Emphasise that students actively engage in writing as an iterative process, as the source illustrates through the example of a student noticing a missing introduction in a peer's essay and then returning to check their own work.

title: Responding to Student Writing Without Overwhelming It
brief: Focus on the challenge of providing feedback without drowning student writing in corrections. Use the source's acknowledgement that the main challenge of providing feedback before assigning a grade is that extra time and effort are required for teachers to provide feedback on drafts and then read and score revised papers. Explain the source's position that teachers should still provide their own corrections and feedback alongside peer input so that students are not relying only on student feedback. Discuss how the teacher in the source material provides feedback around the same time as peer review, creating a balanced approach that keeps the teacher's role meaningful without making it the sole source of correction.

title: Using Correction Checklists: Structure and Purpose
brief: Introduce correction checklists as a practical tool for focusing student attention on specific aspects of their writing. Draw directly on the source's description of the Self-Editing and Peer Editing Checklist for Writing, which covers ten elements: thesis statement, topic sentences, explaining sentences, evidence, interpreting sentences, closing sentences, bridges, conclusion-restatement, conclusion-summary, and conclusion-final thought. Explain the source's claim that checklists can ensure students have addressed important points, help them revise their own drafts, enable more effective and specific peer feedback, and help teachers evaluate work in a more consistent manner. Note that the checklist is used station by station, with each station assigned a different coloured highlighter pen so students can visually track which element they are reviewing.

title: Setting Up a Peer Editing Activity: Step-by-Step Procedure
brief: Walk trainees through the five-step self-editing and peer editing procedure described in the source. Cover each step in sequence: visiting an editing station and following the highlighting directions; using the checklist to self-check that element of the essay and making changes as needed; initialling the checklist after making revisions; asking a classmate to check the same section using the same checklist, with both students discussing and agreeing before initialling; and then moving to the next station and repeating the process. Emphasise the source's point that training is important to explain the purpose of peer feedback, and that letting students know the teacher will review completed peer assessment worksheets can motivate them to take the exercise seriously.

title: Goals and Learner Autonomy: What Peer Review Achieves
brief: Describe the learning goals of the self-editing and peer feedback activity as listed in the source: students notice their own strengths and feel proud of them; they identify missing or weak information; they compare their writing with peers' work; they develop inner criteria for what makes a strong essay; and they encounter different kinds of writing. Explain how the source connects this activity to learner autonomy, noting that students learn they can rely on each other and themselves, can receive good feedback from peers, and are capable of correcting their own writing. Use the source's point that students with weaker writing skills can notice for themselves what needs to be improved, thereby strengthening their skills and becoming more autonomous writers.

title: Challenges, Benefits, and Adapting Peer Review Across Contexts
brief: Present the source's balanced account of the challenges and benefits of peer feedback as an alternative assessment approach. Challenges include the teacher having less control over what happens and the time required to prepare and set up the activity; benefits include students feeling more in control of their own writing and not seeing the teacher as the only authority. Use the source's guidance on adapting the activity for different proficiency levels: for beginning-level students, simpler topics and single words or symbols such as plus signs, minus signs, question marks, or happy and sad faces; for more advanced students, more complex expectations. Close by drawing on the source's statement that overall, students become better writers and more autonomous learners, and that the benefits outweigh the challenges.
